title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the primary mechanical function of the robot arm.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the industrial robot arm?
instructor: The arm positions the end-effector and payload while transferring their loads through the robot joints into the robot body and base.

title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the external loads carried by an extended robot arm.
student: What external loads act on an extended robot arm while it is holding a component stationary?
instructor: The arm carries the weight of the payload, the end-effector, and the arm structure itself.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Describe how the remainder of the robot supports the arm.
student: How is the arm supported by the remainder of the robot?
instructor: The arm is connected to the robot through structural joints and actuators that support and position the arm while transferring loads into the robot body and base.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the force-transfer path from the payload to the floor.
student: Trace the load path from the payload to the floor.
instructor: Payload → gripper/end-effector → robot arm → robot joints and actuators → robot body/base → floor.

title: Effect of Reach
learningObjectives: Explain how payload reach affects bending demand.
student: For the same payload, how would extending the robot arm farther from the base affect the bending demand in the arm? Explain physically.
instructor: The bending demand generally increases because the payload acts through a larger moment arm. Increasing reach therefore increases the moment that must be carried by the arm and supporting joints.

title: Relevant Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify the internal responses relevant to the beam analysis.
student: Which internal mechanical responses are important when evaluating the horizontal arm under vertical loading?
instructor: The important beam responses are internal shear force and bending moment.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the loading and geometry controlling shear and moment.
student: What loading and geometric characteristics would influence the shear-force and bending-moment distributions?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include the payload magnitude and position, arm length, distributed arm/end-effector weight, and locations and directions of the supporting joint or actuator forces.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the industrial robot into an equivalent beam model.
student: Replace the industrial robot with a simplified horizontal beam model that preserves the dominant vertical load path. Show the arm, support locations, end load, distributed weight, and an equivalent actuator force.
instructor: A valid idealization is a horizontal beam carrying a distributed downward load and a concentrated end load, supported by a pin and an inclined two-force actuator. The student should identify the load path and the known direction of the actuator force.
gradingNotes: The detailed labels and dimensions shown in the instructor diagram should be introduced only after the student has attempted the idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions used to create the beam model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real robot arm into the simplified beam model.
instructor: The arm is straight and initially horizontal; loading is static; deformation is small; the distributed weight is uniform; the main support is idealized as a frictionless pin; the inclined actuator is an ideal two-force member; joints and gripper dimensions are neglected; and dynamic, fatigue, local connection, and three-dimensional effects are excluded.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the sequence required to locate the critical bending region.
student: Before performing numerical calculations, describe the mechanics sequence required to locate the critical bending region.
instructor: Replace the distributed load by its resultant for whole-arm equilibrium, solve the actuator force and pin reactions, define a beam coordinate, derive piecewise shear and bending-moment functions, construct the diagrams, and identify the absolute maximum bending moment.

title: Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify restrictions and reactions at A and B.
student: From the instructor reference model, identify the kinematic restrictions and reaction components at A and B.
instructor: The pin at A prevents horizontal and vertical translation but permits rotation, so it provides reactions Ax and Ay. The equivalent actuator at B is a two-force member and applies a force along its own axis.

title: Equivalent Distributed Load
learningObjectives: Replace the uniform load with its equivalent resultant.
student: Replace the uniform load by an equivalent resultant for the whole-arm free-body diagram.
instructor: The loaded length is a + b + L = {{robot_total_length_in}} in. The resultant is W = w(a + b + L) = {{robot_W_lb}} lb and acts at the centroid of the full loaded span. Relative to A, its line of action is {{robot_xW_in}} in to the right.

title: Equivalent Actuator Force
learningObjectives: Determine the equivalent actuator force from moment equilibrium.
student: Use moment equilibrium about A to determine the actuator force and state whether the two-force member is in tension or compression.
instructor: Moment equilibrium gives Byb - W(xW) - P(b + L) = 0, so By = {{robot_By_lb}} lb. With θ = {{robot_theta}}°, FBD = By/sinθ = {{robot_F_BD_lb}} lb. The force on the arm acts upward and to the left; the member therefore acts in {{robot_cylinder_state}}.

title: Pin Reactions
learningObjectives: Determine the reaction components at A.
student: Use force equilibrium to determine the reaction components at A.
instructor: The actuator horizontal component is Bx = FBD cosθ = {{robot_Bx_lb}} lb, so Ax = {{robot_Ax_abs_lb}} lb {{robot_Ax_direction}}. Vertical equilibrium gives Ay + By - W - P = 0, so Ay = {{robot_Ay_abs_lb}} lb {{robot_Ay_direction}}.

title: Beam Coordinate and Regions
learningObjectives: Partition the beam into regions for internal-resultant equations.
student: Let s be measured from the left free end. Identify the beam regions needed for the piecewise equations.
instructor: Region 1: 0 ≤ s ≤ a; Region 2: a ≤ s ≤ a + b; Region 3: a + b ≤ s ≤ a + b + L. Concentrated-force jumps occur at A, B, and C.

title: Shear-Force Functions
learningObjectives: Derive the shear-force function in each beam region.
student: Derive V(s) in each region using upward force as positive.
instructor: V1(s) = -ws. V2(s) = -ws + Ay. V3(s) = -ws + Ay + By, where Ay and By are used with their signed values. At C, the downward payload causes the final jump to zero.

title: Bending-Moment Functions
learningObjectives: Derive the bending-moment function in each beam region.
student: Derive M(s) in each region with M(0) = 0.
instructor: M1(s) = -ws2/2. M2(s) = -ws2/2 + Ay(s - a). M3(s) = -ws2/2 + Ay(s - a) + By[s - (a + b)].

title: Diagram Construction
learningObjectives: Construct and label the shear-force and bending-moment diagrams.
student: Construct the shear-force and bending-moment diagrams and label the key ordinates.
instructor:
The shear diagram is linear between concentrated loads and has jumps at A, B, and C. Its key values are: left free end {{robot_V_left_lb}} lb; A- {{robot_V_A_minus_lb}} lb; A+ {{robot_V_A_plus_lb}} lb; B- {{robot_V_B_minus_lb}} lb; B+ {{robot_V_B_plus_lb}} lb; C- {{robot_V_C_minus_lb}} lb; and C+ {{robot_V_C_plus_lb}} lb.

The moment diagram is quadratic between concentrated loads and continuous at A and B. MA = {{robot_M_A_lbin}} lb·in, MB = {{robot_M_B_lbin}} lb·in, and MC = {{robot_M_C_lbin}} lb·in.

title: Absolute Maximum Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Locate and quantify the absolute maximum bending moment.
student: Determine the absolute maximum bending moment and its location.
instructor: The shear is negative immediately to the left of B and positive immediately to the right, so the bending moment reaches its most negative value at B. The governing signed moment is {{robot_M_signed_max_lbin}} lb·in at {{robot_M_location}}. Therefore |M|max = {{robot_M_abs_max_lbin}} lb·in = {{robot_M_abs_max_lbft}} lb·ft.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Identify the first stress-check location and a way to reduce bending demand.
student: Identify the arm section that should be checked first in a subsequent bending-stress analysis and recommend one mechanics-based change that would reduce the bending demand.
instructor: The section at or immediately adjacent to B should be checked first because it carries the largest absolute bending moment. Reducing the payload or reducing the payload reach directly reduces the bending demand. In the equivalent model, moving the actuator support closer to the payload or increasing its vertical leverage can also reduce the peak moment.
